Abstract—Deep learning demonstrates its efficacy and
potential to solve challenging computer vision problems in
medical and other industrial applications. Federated learn-
ing is a learning paradigm that facilitates collaborative
learning in a federation of users without exchanging actual
data with a single authority like a server. However, federated
learning provides only a basic level of privacy and robust-
ness and is vulnerable to model poisoning and model in-
version attacks in hostile training environments. Hence, in
this article, we propose MediSecFed—a secure framework
for federated learning in a hostile environment. Compared
to the widely used FedAvg, our method relies on simple
and practical ideas from knowledge distillation and model
inversion to ensure additional security and privacy fea-
tures. Our approach achieves knowledge exchange among
participating entities without sharing model parameters as
FedAvg does, thus protecting the privacy of the local data
from the server and significantly reducing communication
costs. We evaluate our method on two chest

and several others) have been developed. Deep learning is now
widely used in industrial applications by utilizing vast amounts
of generated datasets. Recently, the deep learning model has
shown its potential in healthcare applications as a feature ex-
tractor for cancer prediction [1].

huge amount of computation and a vast number of datasets. As

ized through extensive computational programming with large
datasets. In the distributed setting of healthcare applications,
medical data are typically fragmented and private, making it
difficult to create robust results among communities. Different
medical institutions may be able to access only the clinical
records of their respective patient communities. However, these
records are susceptible since they contain patients’ private health
information. Strict regulations and government laws have been
devised to manage the process of obtaining and analyzing such
data. This presents a major hurdle for creating successful, gen-
eralized, deep learning-based models that require varied and
large amounts of medical data. Data sharing among medical
institutions is becoming increasingly desirable to minimize the
shortage and distribution biases of medical data and enhance
model performance on critical tasks.
Moreover, sharing medical data with a third party is a major
concern to the data owner or institution, even if the third party is
well known or anonymous. Besides that, due to the potential con-
flict of interest in each medical institution, it is also impractical to
aggregate sensitive data from IoT devices in different hospitals
to build an efficient model for healthcare diagnostic systems.

Therefore, federated learning (FL) [2] has recently emerged as a
promising solution for this problem in a distributed environment.
The overview of the classical FL scheme is presented in Fig. 1.
It enables training a shared global model using a central server
while retaining all sensitive data in the local medical institution
where it belongs. FL has tremendous potential for connecting
fragmented healthcare data sources while maintaining privacy.
It enables learning from distributed data sources by aggregating
the locally obtained model parameters without transmitting sen-
sitive health data. However, there are major impediments to the
scalable deployment of secure and truly privacy-preserving FL
for sensitive applications. Existing FL algorithms are vulnerable
to adversarial updates [3] and backdoor attacks [4], and they
can expose sensitive information on local datasets [5]. This
jeopardizes personal privacy and has the potential to result in
unforeseen economic and life losses. In some ways, the privacy
issues in FL constitute a significant impediment to the market-
ing and development of industrial artificial intelligence based
applications.
The key challenges in federated training are communica-
tion overheads and client heterogeneity: Training data, as well
as hardware and computing resources, can vary dramatically
between clients, e.g., when training on mobile devices. The
primary goal of the medical data classification problem is to
train a model that can produce good results on the test datasets.
To accomplish this, we train a huge model, which could be an
ensemble of several individual trained models or just a very large
model trained using a regularizer such as a Dropout. Once the
huge model (teacher) is trained, we utilize a process known as
distillation to transfer the complicated knowledge gained by the
huge model to a smaller model (student) that is more suited for
deployment in devices with limited memory and compute power.
The huge model must generalize properly so that when we are
distilling knowledge to the smaller model, it can generalize in
the same way as the large model. Hence, knowledge distillation
(KD) [6], a new technique for compacting and accelerating neu-
ral networks, is developed to maintain comparable performance
while keeping the constraints in mind.
Despite the favorable outcomes, KD techniques rely heavily
on huge amounts of training data to transmit information from
pretrained teacher models to students. However, owing to pri-
vacy or transmission concerns, the training data are sometimes
not shared alongside the pretrained models, rendering these
approaches inapplicable. Another limitation is KD’s reliance on
proxy data, as the selection of proxy data, which requires careful
consideration, is a critical factor in distillation performance.
To solve this issue, data-free KD is proposed [7]. Data-free
KD generally uses the generated surrogate data based on the
large network (teacher) for training a fast and compact (student)
network. Some researchers [7] prefer to generate surrogate data
by using the statistical metadata of the activation in a large
network (teacher).
While model inversion (MI) [8] is another strategy for gen-
erating synthesized data for training student networks, it is a
critical step in the data-free KD process, with the objective of
recovering training data from pretrained teacher models. Student
models may be easily learned using the generated synthetic
data by directly using the data-driven KD methods. Recently, a
generative adversarial network has demonstrated its potential in
image synthesis and translation, becoming a popular choice for
such applications [9]. In general, sensitive and confidential data
in the healthcare domain necessitates security in a distributed
environment. In order to be processed through deep learning
based approaches, data must be centralized, but owing to medical
data privacy regulations, collecting and sharing patients’ data in
a centralized data server is often not feasible. Also, in the case
of a new disease such as COVID-19, there is a lack of vast
amounts of annotated training data at a single site. Therefore,
in this study, we have attempted to tackle the data privacy leak-
age problem due to shared model parameters in traditional FL
algorithms.
Motivation and Contribution: FL ensures a basic level of
privacy by not exchanging the actual data with any other partic-
ipating entity. Yet it trades the model’s parameters with a server.
To subvert the data privacy leakage problem due to shared model
parameters in traditional FL algorithms, we propose a method
called MediSecFed. Our approach takes inspiration from KD
and model inversion literature to build a framework that ensures
good performance without trading off client privacy. Inherently,
our method reduces the communication cost significantly while
preserving privacy. To the best of our knowledge, most of the
works [10]–[13] tackle this issue for natural images, but their use
on computer vision tasks on medical images is unknown. Some
of the assumptions made in the works [10] and [11] are unfair to
the medical domain due to strict regulations, compliance rules,
and the lack of availability of large, labeled datasets. Our ex-
perimentation on the two medical datasets—-COVIDx-8B [14]
and COVIDx-8A [14]—-reveals that our method has better
performance than FedAvg [15] in malicious environments. Our
objective is to showcase a possible research direction for training
a deep learning model for medical application in a secure and
privacy-preserved manner. The main contributions of our article
can be summarized as follows.

nique to obtain the dataset for effective KD in a collab-

II. PRELIMINARIES
In this section, we briefly introduced the terminologies which
are closely related to our work.
A. Knowledge Distillation
KD is a compression scheme, also known as teacher–student
compression, proposed by [16] that allows for the training of
a smaller compact student network under the supervision of a
larger pretrained teacher network or ensemble of networks, with-
out the need for costly computation and storage. In the work [17],
the authors formally introduced and generalized the term “KD,”
which has since become popular among researchers. They tried
to match the softmax activation function of the student’s logit
with the softmax temperature activation function of the large
network (teacher’s) logit. KD is widely used in knowledge
transfer and model compression. However, when compared to
other compression techniques, KD is capable of downsizing the
network without regard for the structural difference between
the teacher and student network model. Furthermore, ensemble
distillation was also studied by the authors where ensemble
of teacher models were considered, and where knowledge was
distilled from the ensemble of network to student by doing an
average of logit of the ensemble networks [18], [19]. Most of
these approaches used real-world data for KD, but they could not
handle cases where distillation data are not readily available. To
overcome the real-world dataset dependency for KD, data-free
KD was proposed in which synthetic data or metadata was used
for KD [20]. DeepInversion [21] has been recently proposed in
the same spirit.
B. Federated KD
The unavailability of large amounts of data, especially for
the medical domain, due to data privacy concerns and legal
constraints, while training a deep neural network in a distributed
computation system is one of the challenging problems. FL
can help to solve this problem to some extent. However, in the
case of FL, model parameters are generally transferred in each
communication round. Sharing a large number of parameters of
deep networks incurs additional computation and communica-
tion costs. In medical domain, data collection and annotation
are critical and costly tasks. Data annotation, particularly for
medical images, necessitates significant effort as well as domain
expertise. Federated KD [22] is thus proposed to address the
aforementioned issues as well as user heterogeneity. It uses
unlabeled data labeled by the teacher model (T) to transfer
information from the teacher model to the small or compact
student model (S). It has the potential to lessen dependency on
labeled data while also ensuring privacy and security. The goal of
federated KD is to reduce the L2 loss between the output logits
of the teacher model (T) and the output logits of the student
(S). During training, the distillation task is used in conjunction
with supervised learning with labeled samples. This objective

D. Model Security and Communication Efficiency
1) Model Security and Poisoning: This section details some
of the security features enjoyed by our method over other al-
gorithms like FedAvg. FedAvg enables multiple data holders to
train a global model without sharing their data but by sharing
their training gradients/parameters [27], [28]. Algorithms like
FedAvg are not robust to attacks like poisoning via label flip poi-
soning or the addition of random noise. Even a single malicious
client can alter the global model. Since a deep learning model can
remember the training data, exchanging the model parameters
with a malicious server violates the desired level of privacy.
Hence, directly exchanging the model parameter/gradients is not
a great idea, especially in the medical domain. On the contrary,
MediSecFed significantly reduces the updates from the model
parameters’ size to its output dimension. As per the work carried
out in [11], a reduction in the size of the updates significantly
boosts the robustness guarantee when robust aggregation algo-
rithms are used. Furthermore, since MediSecFed does not share
the model parameters with the server, the probability of model
inversion attacks is close to zero. Also, unlike FedAvg, MediS-
ecFed does not produce a single global model. Instead, each
client will have the model tailored for its local dataset with some
knowledge shared by the other participants via the KD process.
Finally, the experimental results presented in Section IV reveal
that MediSecFed is relatively robust to poisoning attacks like
random noise addition. All these security and privacy features
offered by our method provide a considerable advantage for
a system deployed in the real world where adversaries try to
hamper the overall performance of the training process.
2) Communication Efficiency: Apart from solid security fea-
tures, our method is communication efficient compared to estab-
lished methods like FedAvg. Consider a simple training environ-
ment with all clients with the same neural network architecture as
ResNet-18. There is a total of 11 million trainable parameters in
ResNet-18. In FedAvg, the trainable parameters are exchanged
in every communication round. Considering the parameters use
floating-point 32 precision, the total size of weights is
4 4 ~ \mathrm { M B }
which has to be uploaded by the client in every communication
round. FedAvg is more demanding for clients with weak network
connections, and the possibility of failing to upload is high
because of the enormous size of the weights. It is highly likely to
have an asymmetric network where upload speed is slower than
download speeds in real-world applications. In MediSecFed, in
every communication round, we send the logits corresponding
to the number of classes in the output layer, which is very low,
mostly in kilobytes (KBs). Our method improves communica-
tion efficiency by reducing the number of parameters shared
from 11 million to just 10 (if the output layer of the neural
network has ten classes).
We believe the above security features and communication
efficiency of our method can open up industrial use cases that
were not possible before with FedAvg.

D. Model Security and Communication Efficiency
1) Model Security and Poisoning: This section details some
of the security features enjoyed by our method over other al-
gorithms like FedAvg. FedAvg enables multiple data holders to
train a global model without sharing their data but by sharing
their training gradients/parameters [27], [28]. Algorithms like
FedAvg are not robust to attacks like poisoning via label flip poi-
soning or the addition of random noise. Even a single malicious
client can alter the global model. Since a deep learning model can
remember the training data, exchanging the model parameters
with a malicious server violates the desired level of privacy.
Hence, directly exchanging the model parameter/gradients is not
a great idea, especially in the medical domain. On the contrary,
MediSecFed significantly reduces the updates from the model
parameters’ size to its output dimension. As per the work carried
out in [11], a reduction in the size of the updates significantly
boosts the robustness guarantee when robust aggregation algo-
rithms are used. Furthermore, since MediSecFed does not share
the model parameters with the server, the probability of model
inversion attacks is close to zero. Also, unlike FedAvg, MediS-
ecFed does not produce a single global model. Instead, each
client will have the model tailored for its local dataset with some
knowledge shared by the other participants via the KD process.
Finally, the experimental results presented in Section IV reveal
that MediSecFed is relatively robust to poisoning attacks like
random noise addition. All these security and privacy features
offered by our method provide a considerable advantage for
a system deployed in the real world where adversaries try to
hamper the overall performance of the training process.
2) Communication Efficiency: Apart from solid security fea-
tures, our method is communication efficient compared to estab-
lished methods like FedAvg. Consider a simple training environ-
ment with all clients with the same neural network architecture as
ResNet-18. There is a total of 11 million trainable parameters in
ResNet-18. In FedAvg, the trainable parameters are exchanged
in every communication round. Considering the parameters use
floating-point 32 precision, the total size of weights is
4 4 ~ \mathrm { M B }
which has to be uploaded by the client in every communication
round. FedAvg is more demanding for clients with weak network
connections, and the possibility of failing to upload is high
because of the enormous size of the weights. It is highly likely to
have an asymmetric network where upload speed is slower than
download speeds in real-world applications. In MediSecFed, in
every communication round, we send the logits corresponding
to the number of classes in the output layer, which is very low,
mostly in kilobytes (KBs). Our method improves communica-
tion efficiency by reducing the number of parameters shared
from 11 million to just 10 (if the output layer of the neural
network has ten classes).
We believe the above security features and communication
efficiency of our method can open up industrial use cases that
were not possible before with FedAvg.

KD and model inversion to perform learning in a collaborative
training environment with no risk of exposing the local model or
the data to a server or a third party. Furthermore, our extensive
analysis of two chest

6) Sharing Generated Data: As our method relies on data
generated using the model inversion process, distributing gen-
erated data to all the participants can be challenging. In an
industrial environment where it is highly likely for devices to
have weaker upload speeds relative to download speed, our
method is indeed efficient and effective. As distillation data are
generated and distributed by the server, we assume that the server
is honest and does not interfere with the model inversion process.
In industrial situations where the central server cannot be trusted,
one can generate data locally on each client if sufficient comput-
ing is available. All the clients can use the same initial seed to
generate the same set of distillation images. The actual working
framework for sharing the metadata is beyond the scope of this
article. Still, we see a clear possibility of using block-chain to
share the sensitive metadata so that the server cannot manipulate
the inversion process.
V. CONCLUSION
In this article, we have designed a new method called MediS-
ecFed, which has leveraged the combination of techniques from
KD and model inversion to perform learning in a collaborative
training environment with no risk of exposing the local model or
the data to a server or a third party. Furthermore, our extensive
